name: Labradorite
physical: Kept nearby for comfort during stressful times
summary: Labradorite is the grey feldspar with a flash of electric blue and gold, a stone of magic, transformation and intuition in the crystal tradition.
intro: Labradorite looks dull grey until you tilt it, and then the whole surface erupts in electric blue, green, gold, or copper. The effect is called labradorescence and it comes from thin lamellae inside the feldspar that bend and scatter light. The stone belongs to the plagioclase series, between albite and anorthite. It was first described from Labrador, in Canada, and today the best stones come from Madagascar and Finland. Labradorite is almost always cut as a cabochon or polished slab so the flash shows well. Many people consider it one of the most magical-looking stones, and it is a firm favorite among jewelry makers.
history: The name labradorite comes from the Labrador Peninsula, where Moravian missionaries encountered the stone around 1770. The Inuit and Innu peoples told stories of the Northern Lights being trapped inside the rocks, and that legend lingers in many labradorite descriptions. A warrior was said to have freed most of the lights with a spear, leaving some behind in the stone. Finnish stones with especially vivid color were later sold as spectrolite after deposits were found near Ylämaa in the early twentieth century. In Russia, labradorite became popular as an ornamental facing stone. Today it is mined in several countries and is a staple of the jewelry trade.
meaning: Labradorite is regarded as a stone of mystery and transformation. Its flash is said to reveal what lies beneath the surface, encouraging you to trust your intuition and to look inward. Crystal practitioners link it to the Third Eye and Crown chakras and to the Throat chakra for speaking inner truths. Many people reach for labradorite when they are in a period of change, saying it helps them hold steady while they sort out what comes next. It is also used as a shield in crowded or draining spaces, soothing the feeling of absorbing other people's moods. Writers and artists often keep it as a muse because it seems to loosen the imagination. Its energy is described as subtle and protective, never loud.
howToUse: Hold a labradorite palm stone during meditation and tilt it slowly to watch the flash, which gives your attention an easy anchor. Wear it as a pendant or ring when moving through crowds, or keep a small stone in your pocket at events. Place a slab on your desk as a creative muse, or set one on the nightstand for dream work. In grids it pairs well with amethyst and clear quartz for intuition layouts. Some people keep a piece in the home entry as a gentle energetic guard. Use it during journaling when you want to explore a decision.
care: Labradorite is Mohs 6 to 6.5 with cleavage in two directions, so avoid knocks and store it apart from harder stones. A brief rinse in lukewarm water is fine; dry it quickly and skip ultrasonic cleaners. Moonlight, sound, or smoke are the gentlest ways to cleanse it, and a full Moon windowsill recharge is traditional. It is stable in sunlight, but hot cars or radiators can stress fractures. Polish only with a soft cloth to keep the flash bright.
identify: Genuine labradorite shows a distinct flash that appears only at certain angles, turning from dark grey to vivid blue, green, or gold as you rotate it. Glass imitations show a fixed glow in all directions and may have bubbles. Some cheap pieces are coated with a thin layer to enhance color, and some are sold as black moonstone. Spectrolite is the Finnish material with a full rainbow of color. A cloudy, whitish moonstone-like glow without spectral color is more likely rainbow moonstone.

faq.a: Labradorite is traditionally used for intuition, transformation, and protection of the aura. People hold it during change, creative work, or crowded situations when they want a sense of steady, inner magic.

The flash is called labradorescence. Thin internal layers in the feldspar bend and reflect light, so color appears only at certain viewing angles. It is a natural optical effect and not a coating or dye in genuine stones.

A quick rinse in lukewarm water is fine, but do not soak it or use ultrasonic cleaners. Labradorite has cleavage and can chip with knocks, so dry it right away and store it apart from harder gemstones.
